why:
Viscosity is expressed through the coefficient of viscosity \(\eta\). Section 10.8.3 of this chapter gives its SI unit as \(\mathrm{N\ s\ m^{-2}}\) and states that in the CGS system \(\eta\) is measured in **poise**, with \(1\ \text{poise} = 1\ \mathrm{g\ cm^{-1}\ s^{-1}} = 10^{-1}\ \mathrm{kg\ m^{-1}\ s^{-1}}\). Poise is therefore the only viscosity unit in the list.

The other three are ruled out on dimensions alone : the dyne is the CGS unit of **force** and the newton the SI unit of **force**, so both are \(\mathrm{M\,L\,T^{-2}}\), while viscosity is \(\mathrm{M\,L^{-1}\,T^{-1}}\); and the gram is a unit of **mass**, \(\mathrm{M}\) alone. None of the three can measure the internal friction between the layers of a flowing liquid.

The ideal gas equation is \(\mathrm{PV} = n\mathrm{RT}\) (Eq. 10.15). The question fixes the amount of gas at \(n = 2\ \mathrm{mol}\), so substituting that value gives \(\mathrm{PV} = 2\mathrm{RT}\), which is the relation that holds specifically for two moles.

\(\mathrm{PV} = \mathrm{RT}\) is the equation for **one** mole, i.e. \(n = 1\), and it under-states the product \(\mathrm{PV}\) by a factor of two here. \(\mathrm{PV} = \mathrm{T}\) cannot hold at all — \(\mathrm{PV}\) has the dimensions of energy while \(\mathrm{T}\) is a temperature, so the two sides are not even the same kind of quantity.

[Note : the remaining alternative, \(\mathrm{PV} = n\mathrm{RT}\), is the general ideal gas equation. It is true for two moles, but it is equally true for any other amount and so makes no use of the information the question supplies; the alternative asked for is the one that specialises the equation to \(n = 2\).]

Section 10.2 states the order plainly : intermolecular forces are strong in solids, less strong in liquids and very weak in gases. Reading that for a liquid gives two facts at once — the forces in a liquid are **greater than** those in a gas, and **less than** those in a solid. Both of the first two alternatives are therefore correct statements, and the alternative that asserts both of them together is the complete answer.

The remaining alternative, that the forces in a liquid are greater than in solids, reverses the chapter's order and is false; it is also refuted by Table 10.1, which records that a solid has a definite shape while a liquid takes the shape of its container — behaviour a liquid could not show if its molecules were held more tightly than a solid's.

An ideal gas is defined in section 10.7 by three properties, the second of which is that there are **no interactive forces between the molecules**; Table 10.6 repeats it as 'no attraction or repulsion between the gas molecules'. So the interactive forces in an ideal gas are nil — which is exactly why an ideal gas obeys \(\mathrm{PV} = n\mathrm{RT}\) at every pressure and temperature and can never be liquefied.

Forces that are *small* but non-zero describe a **real** gas at low pressure and high temperature, where the chapter says the behaviour merely approaches ideality; *large* forces describe a real gas at high pressure and low temperature, the condition under which the chapter says liquefaction occurs; and forces the *same as those of real gases* would leave nothing to distinguish the two, contradicting the whole of Table 10.6.

The temperature is constant and the mass of gas is fixed, so Boyle's law applies : \(\mathrm{P_1V_1} = \mathrm{P_2V_2}\) (Eq. 10.3).

\(\mathrm{V_2} = \dfrac{\mathrm{P_1V_1}}{\mathrm{P_2}} = \dfrac{105\ \mathrm{kPa} \times 22.4\ \mathrm{dm^3}}{210\ \mathrm{kPa}} = 11.2\ \mathrm{dm^3}\)

The pressure is doubled, so the volume must be halved. The value \(44.8\ \mathrm{dm^3}\) is the volume **doubled**, which is what would happen if the pressure had been halved rather than doubled; \(22.4\ \mathrm{dm^3}\) leaves the volume unchanged, which would require the pressure to be unchanged too; and \(5.6\ \mathrm{dm^3}\) is one quarter of the original volume and would need the pressure to rise to \(420\ \mathrm{kPa}\).

Write the ideal gas equation for a known mass \(m\) of gas of molar mass \(\mathrm{M}\), using \(n = m/\mathrm{M}\) :

\(\mathrm{PV} = \dfrac{m}{\mathrm{M}}\mathrm{RT} \qquad \Rightarrow \qquad \dfrac{m}{\mathrm{V}} = d = \dfrac{\mathrm{PM}}{\mathrm{RT}}\)

This is the chapter's Eq. (10.19). Now test the three statements against it.

i. At constant temperature and pressure the factor \(\mathrm{P}/\mathrm{RT}\) is a constant, so \(d \propto \mathrm{M}\) — density really is directly proportional to molar mass. True.

ii. Direct proportionality with a positive constant is an increasing relation, so of two gases measured under the same conditions the denser one must have the larger molar mass. True, and it is only a restatement of the first.

iii. Rearranging the same equation gives \(\mathrm{M} = \dfrac{d\mathrm{RT}}{\mathrm{P}}\), the chapter's Eq. (10.20), so knowing the density, the temperature and the pressure is exactly enough to obtain the molar mass. True.

All three statements are correct, so the alternative that says so is the answer. No single one of them can be selected on its own, because each of the other two is also true.
